questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm executes processes in the order they arrive?
questions.explanation: First-Come First-Served schedules processes in arrival order. It's simple but can cause long waiting times if short processes arrive after long ones.

questions.question: What scheduling algorithm selects the process with the shortest burst time?
questions.explanation: Shortest Job First minimizes average waiting time by executing shortest processes first. However, it can cause starvation for long processes.

questions.question: Which algorithm assigns each process a fixed time quantum?
questions.explanation: Round Robin gives each process a time quantum. If the process doesn't finish, it's moved to the end of the ready queue.

questions.question: What scheduling approach allows processes to be interrupted?
questions.explanation: Preemptive scheduling can interrupt running processes to switch to higher-priority or waiting processes. This prevents CPU monopolization.

questions.question: Which metric measures the time from submission to completion?
questions.explanation: Turnaround time is the total time from arrival to completion, including waiting, execution, and I/O time. It measures overall process time.

questions.question: What problem occurs when low-priority processes never execute?
questions.explanation: Starvation occurs when processes wait indefinitely because higher-priority processes keep arriving. Aging can prevent this by gradually increasing priority.

questions.question: Which algorithm can lead to the convoy effect?
questions.explanation: FCFS suffers from the convoy effect when short processes wait behind long ones. This increases average waiting time significantly.

questions.question: What scheduling uses multiple queues with different priorities?
questions.explanation: Multilevel queue scheduling assigns processes to different queues based on characteristics. Each queue can have its own scheduling algorithm.

questions.question: What technique prevents starvation by increasing waiting process priority?
questions.explanation: Aging gradually increases the priority of waiting processes. This ensures long-waiting processes eventually get CPU time despite low initial priority.

questions.question: Which algorithm is optimal for minimizing average waiting time?
questions.explanation: Shortest Job First provides optimal average waiting time by always executing the shortest remaining process. However, it requires knowing burst times in advance.

questions.question: Which metric measures the time from submission until the first response is produced?
questions.explanation: Response time measures how quickly the system first responds after submission. It matters most in interactive and time-sharing systems.

questions.question: What is the duration of continuous CPU execution by a process called?
questions.explanation: Burst time is uninterrupted CPU execution between I/O requests. Algorithms like SJF base their decisions on its predicted length.

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm always runs the ready process with the highest priority?
questions.explanation: Priority scheduling runs the highest-priority ready process first. Without aging, low-priority processes can starve indefinitely.

questions.question: What is the preemptive version of SJF called?
questions.explanation: SRTF preempts the running process when a new arrival has a shorter remaining time. It produces the optimal average waiting time.

questions.question: What does Round Robin degenerate into when the time quantum is very large?
questions.explanation: With a huge quantum, every process finishes within its slice in arrival order. Round Robin effectively becomes FCFS.

questions.question: What happens to context switch overhead when the Round Robin quantum is too small?
questions.explanation: A tiny quantum means the CPU spends most of its time context switching. Overhead grows while real work done per quantum shrinks.

questions.question: Which algorithm allows processes to move between queues based on their observed behavior?
questions.explanation: Multilevel feedback queues promote or demote processes based on observed behavior. This adapts to I/O-bound versus CPU-bound jobs.

questions.question: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8, P2 at 1 with burst 4, and P3 at 2 with burst 2. Under non-preemptive SJF, which process runs second?
questions.explanation: P1 runs first because it's the only arrival at time 0. At time 8, P3 (burst 2) is chosen over P2 (burst 4) under SJF.

questions.question: Under FCFS, P1 (burst 24), P2 (burst 3), and P3 (burst 3) arrive in that order. What is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: Waiting times are 0, 24, and 27, averaging 17 ms. This is the classic FCFS convoy effect where short jobs wait behind a long one.

questions.question: If the same three processes are instead ordered P2, P3, P1 under FCFS, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: With short jobs first, waiting times are 0, 3, and 6, averaging 3 ms. Arrival ordering dramatically changes FCFS performance.

questions.question: Which real-time scheduling algorithm selects the task with the nearest absolute deadline?
questions.explanation: EDF always runs the task closest to its deadline. It's optimal for single-processor dynamic-priority real-time scheduling.

questions.question: Which component gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the scheduler?
questions.explanation: The dispatcher performs the context switch and jumps to the selected process. Dispatch latency measures this switch time.

questions.question: Which scheduling criterion counts the number of processes completed per unit of time?
questions.explanation: Throughput counts completed processes per time unit. Higher throughput indicates the system finishes more work.

questions.question: In a multilevel feedback queue, which queue usually has the smallest time quantum?
questions.explanation: Top queues favor interactive tasks with small quanta for fast response. Lower queues get larger quanta for CPU-bound work.

questions.question: Which type of processes are most likely to starve under SJF scheduling?
questions.explanation: Long CPU-bound jobs starve under SJF if short jobs keep arriving. Their waiting time can grow without bound.

questions.question: What technique schedules a set of related threads to run simultaneously on multiple CPUs?
questions.explanation: Gang scheduling runs related threads together on multiple CPUs. It keeps tightly-coupled parallel threads from stalling each other.

questions.question: P1 arrives at 0 (burst 10), P2 at 1 (burst 2), and P3 at 2 (burst 3). Under preemptive SJF (SRTF), which process finishes last?
questions.explanation: P2 runs 1-3, P3 runs 3-6, then P1 resumes and finishes at 15; the short arrivals keep preempting the long job.

questions.question: Three processes each with burst 3 arrive at time 0. With Round Robin and quantum 2, what is the average turnaround time?
questions.explanation: Completion times are 7, 8, and 9, so average turnaround is 24/3 = 8 ms.

questions.question: A CPU-bound process exhausts its full quantum on every run under a multilevel feedback queue. What does the scheduler do to it?
options: Promotes it to a higher queue
Demotes it to a lower-priority queue
Moves it to a real-time class
questions.explanation: MLFQ demotes processes that consume their whole quantum, reserving fast queues for interactive, short-burst work.

questions.question: A high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task while medium-priority tasks keep preempting it. Which mechanism resolves this?
questions.explanation: Priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder's priority to the waiter's level, ending unbounded blocking - the Mars Pathfinder fix.

questions.question: P1 (burst 24), P2 (burst 3), and P3 (burst 3) all arrive at time 0. Under non-preemptive SJF, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: SJF orders them P2, P3, P1 with waits of 0, 3, and 6, averaging 3 ms versus 17 ms under FCFS order.
